scenes.name: Las bandas soul y los «supergrupos»
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras EWF, Rufus y los Commodores las discográficas querían bandas: la «banda soul», versión blanda de la banda funk, unidades completas que podían soltar un groove monstruoso pero se producían como grupos pop. Los Brothers Johnson, descubiertos por Quincy Jones (el bajo de Louis Johnson), triunfaron con Look Out for #1 y Right on Time; Blam! (1978) fue su último funk antes del disco-pop de Lite Up the Nite. Heatwave, sexteto multirracial de Alemania con Rod Temperton y los Wilder de Dayton; L.T.D. con Jeffrey Osborne; Frankie Beverly y Maze (de Filadelfia a California, apadrinados por Marvin Gaye), cinco discos de oro de funk suave; Rose Royce, el vehículo de Norman Whitfield (Car Wash). Off the Wall (1979) de Michael Jackson unió con Quincy Jones, Temperton y Louis Johnson todos los elementos de moda sin perder el groove. Bill Berry los llamó en Ebony (1978) «supergrupos»: espectáculos de estadio de fervor casi religioso, como las giras Earth de P-Funk que lanzaron a Cameo, Slave, Rick James y Bootsy. En 1980 casi todos se habían deshecho o pasado al pop.

podcast.title: Departure from R.E.M.
podcast.body: After rejoining R.E.M. later in 1995 following his aneurysm, Berry found that "things just weren't the same." He announced his departure in November 1997, stating a desire for a life change after 17 years with the band and "pounding the tub since I was 9 years old." "I'm ready to do something else."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: On-Stage Brain Aneurysm
podcast.body: On March 1, 1995, Bill Berry suffered a brain aneurysm on stage while performing falsetto background vocals for the song "Tongue." This led to emergency brain surgery and months of recovery. "Then came a transformative moment on March 1st, 1995, when he suffered a brain aneurism on stage while he was in the middle of singing some falsetto background vocals to a song called Tongue."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Pre-Law Background and Multi-Instrumentalist
podcast.body: Bill Berry was a founding member of R.E.M. and was studying pre-law at the University of Georgia in Athens. He played a variety of instruments and co-wrote several of the band's hits, including "Everybody Hurts" and "Man on the Moon." "He was a founding member of the band, while in pre-law at the University of Georgia in Athens."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Retirement as Gentleman Farmer
podcast.body: Bill Berry retired to a 60-acre hay farm in Watkinsville, Georgia, a property his girlfriend purchased in the late 1980s as an investment. He embraced rural life, driving a tractor and caring for sheep, although now a caretaker manages most farm duties, and Berry occasionally tends a garden. "Gentleman Farmer. Bill retired to a hay farm in Watkinsville, Georgia at the end of a long-laid off-old Farmington Road."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bill Berry's Near-Fatal Tick Bite (May 1989)
xref.body: While R.E.M. was on tour in Germany in May 1989, supporting the "Green Album," drummer Bill Berry fell severely ill shortly after arriving in Munich. Initially suspected to be bronchitis or measles due to a rash, his condition worsened with hallucinations and fluctuating consciousness. Despite doctors' panic and a "huge buffet of antibiotics," the cause remained unknown until one doctor's blind prescription of tetracycline proved effective. Bill's doctor in Athens, Georgia, later diagnosed Rocky Mountain spotted fever, which Bill had contracted from a tick bite while gardening at home a week prior, and whose week-long incubation period had led to symptoms emerging during the tour. "Bill varies near fatal bug bites"

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7

xref.title: Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever – April 1989, Munich, Near-Fatal Illness Misidentified by European Doctors
xref.body: In April 1989, during a European tour, Bill Berry collapsed on stage in Munich with a fever of 103°F, chills, muscle aches, severe headache, nausea, red eyes, and a characteristic rash spreading from his wrists and ankles. German doctors, uncertain of the cause, prescribed tetracycline — the only antibiotic effective against Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever, a tick-borne illness virtually unknown in Europe that Berry had almost certainly contracted while gardening before the tour. Had the German doctors chosen penicillin (the standard first choice), Berry would have received no benefit and might have suffered organ failure, coma, and death. The correct diagnosis was only confirmed after his recovery. "It wasn't until later that it was determined that Bill had come down with something called Rocky Mountain Spotted Fever."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: 1995 World Tour Incident
xref.body: In January 1995, R.E.M. embarked on their first world tour in six years, beginning in Australia and moving through Asia before reaching Europe. During a show on March 1, 1995, at the Demali Ice Rink in Lausanne, Switzerland, drummer Bill Berry collapsed on stage about 90 minutes into the gig while singing a falsetto part in the song "Tongue." "During that show, Bill developed a bad headache... And then about 90 minutes into the gig as he was singing the falsetto part in a song called Tung, Bill recalls feeling like somebody dropped the bowling ball on his head."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bill Berry's Brain Aneurysms (March 1995)
xref.body: On March 1, 1995, during a Monster Tour stop in Lausanne, Switzerland, ninety minutes into the set, Bill Berry was suddenly afflicted by a headache so intense he described it as if "somebody had dropped the bowling ball on a skull," and he had to be carried off stage. Initially thought to be a severe migraine caused by stress and the high altitude of the Swiss Alps, a subsequent CAT scan revealed two potentially fatal brain aneurysms. Bill underwent emergency brain surgery and endured an eight-week recovery period, during which there were serious concerns about potential brain damage affecting his ability to speak or remember. "Bill was rushed in for emergency brain surgery and he spent eight long weeks recovering."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 7

xref.title: Dual Brain Aneurysms – March 1, 1995, Lausanne, Switzerland, Emergency Surgery; Tour Resumed May 15
xref.body: Ninety minutes into the 27th show of the Monster world tour — which had started on November 13, 1994 in Perth, Australia — drummer Bill Berry felt as if "somebody dropped a bowling ball on his head" and had to be carried from the stage in Lausanne, Switzerland. He had suffered not one but two potentially fatal brain aneurysms. Emergency brain surgery was performed, and Berry spent eight weeks recovering with the outcome uncertain. The tour was postponed; it resumed on May 15 in San Francisco. To demonstrate the band's dark humor about the episode, the tour program subsequently featured an X-ray of Bill's head showing where the aneurysms had been. "It was not one, but two potentially fatal brain aneurysms."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bill Berry's Brain Aneurysm and Surgery
xref.body: Following his collapse on stage in Switzerland, Bill Berry was hospitalized. An MRI revealed not one, but two aneurysms on the right side of his brain, one of which had ruptured. He underwent a craniotomy where part of his skull was removed, performed by a world-renowned surgeon. Berry suffered no lasting effects on his brain function or motor skills. "an MRI revealed that there was not one but two aneurysms on the right side of his brain. One had ruptured and the other was about two. It was Russian Dissertry where he underwent a criniotomy."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Bill Berry's Departure and New Life
xref.body: The brain aneurysm incident served as a significant wake-up call for Bill Berry. In 1997, two years after the event, he resigned from R.E.M. and has since been living in Georgia, where he works as a gentleman hay farmer. "The incident served as something as a wake-up call for Bill. In 1997 he resigned from the band and lives in Georgia as a gentleman hay farmer."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Departure of Bill Berry (Year Unspecified)
xref.body: Bill Berry, the band's original drummer, quit R.E.M. to become a hay farmer. The band continued as a three-piece for 14 years after his departure, but their success was mixed, and they were "never the same" without him. "Bill Berry, their original drummer, quit to become a hay farmer."

xref.title: Formation Anecdote
xref.body: R.E.M.'s origins began when record store clerk Peter Buck initiated a conversation with art student Michael Stipe, who was often seeking out unusual 12-inch singles. Inspired by the success of friends like The B-52s, Peter and Michael later connected with Mike Mills and Bill Berry, two musicians from Macon, Georgia, to form the band. "a record store clerk named Peter Buck struck up a conversation with an art student who was always looking for strange 12-inch singles, and his name was Michael Steip."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Formation and First Gig
xref.body: Guitarist Peter Buck, a record store clerk, struck up a conversation with art student Michael Stipe, who was often looking for strange 12-inch singles. Encouraged by the success of their friends, The B-52s, Peter and Michael recruited bassist Mike Mills and drummer Bill Berry, both from Macon, Georgia. Their first gig was at a friend's birthday party in a deconsecrated church in Athens on April 5th, 1980. "Shortly after the B-52s began to attract attention, a record store clerk named Peter Buck struck up a conversation with an art student who was always looking for strange 12-inch singles. His name was Michael Steip, encouraged by the success of their friends, the B-52s."

xref.title: Founding Member's Health Scare and Departure
xref.body: Founding member Bill Berry, who was studying pre-law at the University of Georgia, suffered a brain aneurysm on stage on March 1, 1995. Although he rejoined the band after surgery, he ultimately left in November 1997, citing a desire for a life change after 17 years. "I loved my 17 years with REM, but I'm ready to move on to a different phase of my life."

xref.title: Tour Interruption and Recovery
xref.body: After Bill Berry's emergency surgery, all R.E.M. shows were canceled for over two months. Berry recovered in the hospital for about a month, with the band members keeping him company and even smuggling in fresh donuts. The band returned to the stage with Berry on May 15, 1995, in Mountain View, California, and the official tour program for that leg featured an image of Bill's brain showing the aneurysms. "All shows were canceled until May 15th 1995 when Bill in the band returned to the stage in Mountain View California. The official program for that part of the tour featured an image of Bill's brain showing the aneurysms."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

xref.title: Tour Support Drummer for R.E.M.
xref.body: When R.E.M. drummer Bill Berry collapsed on stage in March 1995 due to a brain aneurysm, the drummer from Grant Lee Buffalo, who were the support act, stepped in to finish the show. "The drummer from support acts Grant Lee Buffalo took over."
